title: External Enablement Across Types of Environmental Change: Experimental Evidence on Onset Variance Effects
authors: Jiyoung Kim; Per Davidsson; Denis A. Grégoire
affiliations: University of Queensland, Queensland, Australia; Jönköping International Business School, Jönköping, Sweden; Australian Centre for Entrepreneurship Research, Queensland University of Technology, Queensland, Australia; HEC Montréal, Québec, Canada
abstract: A growing research stream applies the external enablement framework (EEF) to capture how macroenvironmental changes benefit entrepreneurial pursuits. To refine and nuance the EEF’s guidance of future research in this domain, we examine the provisionally suggested structural relationships among its constructs. Combining between-subjects experiments and think-aloud protocols, we show that variance in the characteristics of macroenvironmental changes—specifically, their gradual versus radical onset—influences expectations of enablement and does so similarly across types of change. Our results also uncover relationships between macroenvironmental changes and agents beyond what the EEF explicates. We discuss implications for future research on macroenvironmental impact on business.

title: Excessive Heat and Correctional Officer Turnover: Evidence From Texas
authors: Benjamin Goehring; Jacob Harris
affiliations: Frank Batten School of Leadership and Public Policy University of Virginia Charlottesville Virginia USA; Department of Criminal Justice and Criminology, Andrew Young School of Policy Studies Georgia State University Atlanta Georgia USA
abstract: ABSTRACT Correctional work is difficult, dangerous, and hot. Many US prisons lack air‐conditioning, resulting in sweltering conditions for both incarcerated people and the street‐level bureaucrats tasked with their supervision. We examine the effect of working in the summer heat without air‐conditioning on correctional officer turnover using personnel records of nearly 60,000 Texas Department of Criminal Justice (TDCJ) employees across 68 prisons between 2010 and 2023. We demonstrate that, among the least‐experienced frontline employees before the onset of COVID‐19, the difference in the probability of departing between those working in prisons without and with air‐conditioning is, on average, 0.33 percentage points larger in the hottest months than in the coolest—an approximately 12% change relative to the baseline departure rate. Back‐of‐the‐envelope estimates suggest that installing air‐conditioning to combat understaffing is comparable in cost to raising salaries, the TDCJ's standard response to high turnover.

title: Democratic Organizing and Contemporary Managerial Talent Markets: Internal Promotion or External Hiring?
authors: Aleksandra Gregoric; Takao Kato; Casper B. L. Larsen
affiliations: Copenhagen Business School, Department of Accounting, Center for Corporate Governance and Owner-Managed Firms, Frederiksberg, Denmark; Colgate University, Department of Economics, Hamilton, New York, United States; Copenhagen Business School, Department of Accounting, Center for Corporate Governance, Frederiksberg, Capital Region, Denmark
abstract: We develop and empirically examine a theoretical framework explaining the relationship between democratic organizing and firms’ propensity to staff management positions through internal promotion rather than external hiring. Conventionally, the advantages of promoting through internal labor markets (ILM) have rested on the assumption that workers value intra-firm careers and anticipate remaining with the same employer for a longer term. These advantages may prove harder to attain in contemporary labor markets, given that declining tenure and workers’ growing preference for inter-firm careers possibly reduce the information advantage of ILM and undermine internal candidate retention. We propose that firms with more democratic organizing are less susceptible to these ILM challenges, enjoy higher benefits from recruiting internally and are thus more likely to fill management positions through internal promotion. Using longitudinal employer-employee linked data for Danish firms from 2001 to 2017, we find that firms with worker board representation (WBR), one form of more democratic organizing, are more likely than firms without WBR to fill management positions through internal promotion rather than external hiring. This association is stronger where (i) worker representatives have broader intra-firm experience and are more likely to possess promotion-relevant information; (ii) more managers and professionals have peers serving as worker representatives on the board. These results are consistent with a higher economic viability of internal promotion in firms with more democratic organizing, and largely inconsistent with the conventional account of powerful workers distorting firms’ hiring choices. Interviews with worker directors and human resource professionals illustrate the proposed mechanisms.

title: Online Job Selection: Reward Rate vs. Remaining Value
authors: Mohammad Reza Aminian; Will Ma; Linwei Xin
affiliations: Booth School of Business, University of Chicago, Chicago, Illinois 60637; Graduate School of Business, Columbia University, New York, New York 10027; School of Operations Research and Information Engineering, Cornell University, Ithaca, New York 14853
abstract: High-throughput systems, such as cloud spot markets, adaptive large language model inference, and order consolidation in logistics, operate under capacity constraints. In these settings, decision makers must allocate fixed resources among a stream of requests with heterogeneous reward rates and service durations. A critical tension arises when capacity is saturated; the system must decide whether to continue serving an active job to harvest its remaining value or to preempt it in favor of a new arrival. This trade-off is especially subtle when a new job offers a lower immediate reward rate but a longer service duration, potentially outweighing a high-rate job near completion. To address this challenge, we introduce a general and parsimonious online allocation framework for capacity-constrained resources, where preemption is nonresumable and yields partial rewards. This abstraction captures the essential dynamics of modern resource management problems, including but not limited to those discussed earlier. We derive intuitive index-based policies and provide constant-factor competitive-ratio guarantees for their performance without requiring any forecasts of future demand. In particular, we show that two naive index-based policies have competitive ratios of 1/2 and [Formula: see text]. Our main methodological contribution is to develop a flexible framework for defining “quasiutilities” that couples the states of an online algorithm versus an offline algorithm, which reduces the design of online index-based policies to an offline geometrical problem. The framework allows us to optimize the index function, leading to an exponential-index-based policy that has an improved competitive ratio of 0.68. We also consider various extensions and prove that most of our analyses are tight. Finally, we conduct a concise numerical study to demonstrate the strong empirical performance of the proposed policies under nonworst-case stochastic demand sequences. title: Machine Learning Vast Dynamic Conditional Covariance Matrices: The Spirit of “Divide and Conquer”
authors: Zhoufan Zhu; Ke Zhu
affiliations: Wang Yanan Institute for Studies in Economics, Xiamen University, Xiamen 361005, China; and Department of Finance, School of Economics, Xiamen University, Xiamen 361005, China; Department of Statistics and Actuarial Science, The University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong
abstract: Large-scale portfolio selection requires accurate forecasts of high-dimensional dynamic conditional covariance matrices (CCMs). This task is challenging because the number of covariance elements grows quickly with the number of assets, whereas the available time-series observations are limited and noisy. In this paper, we propose a novel graph-based quantiled (GRAND) CCM estimator in the spirit of “divide and conquer.” By extracting information from the extensive asset features, the GRAND method leverages a new graph-based deep learning network, called the self-grouping autoencoder (SGA), to learn the conditional quantiles of returns. Using those learned conditional quantiles, the GRAND method further learns (co)variances of CCM element-wisely via the quantiled conditional moment (QCM) method, and finally, it makes the resulting assembled CCM estimator positive semidefinite through a projection. Because of the use of the SGA network and the QCM method in an element-wise way, the GRAND method is blessing dimensionality in learning the CCM of a large-scale portfolio, while keeping the computation manageable and maintaining causal semantics. From an extensive empirical analysis of the Chinese stock market, we show that the GRAND method can produce much better tangency portfolios than its competitors, and provide dynamic causal graphs to study variance and quantile connectedness of all stocks for interpreting systemic risk and forecasting the business cycle. This paper was accepted by Kay Giesecke, finance. title: When GenAI Increases Inequality: Evidence from a University Debating Competition
authors: Antonio Roldán-Monés
affiliations: School of Politics, Economics and Global Affairs (IESPEGA), IE University, 28046 Madrid, Spain
abstract: Research on Generative AI (GenAI) and work reports both productivity-compressing and inequality-expanding effects, leaving open a central question for organizations: Who benefits from GenAI and on which specific tasks? I address this question through a randomized controlled trial in competitive university debating, where participants are randomly assigned access to GenAI. Although most previous experimental work examines the impact of GenAI on written activities and across individuals, this setting allows me to study the impact of GenAI on a knowledge-intensive spoken activity and to identify heterogeneous effects across subtasks. I find that GenAI expands performance inequality in this setting. Consistent with recent theories on GenAI and work, results show that high-ability participants experience significantly larger gains from GenAI usage than their lower-ability counterparts in judgment-intensive subtasks, whereas lower-ability individuals only improve their performance in less expert components of debating, where GenAI can be used as a substitute. If these inequality-expanding effects generalize to similar spoken settings where complex ideas must be internalized and explained, rather than simply written, they would have important implications for understanding the impact of GenAI on work and inequality. This paper was accepted by Maria Guadalupe, business strategy. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.01063 .

title: Scalable Just-in-Time Price Elasticity Estimation
authors: Jingbo Wang; Yufeng Huang
affiliations: Department of Marketing, Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong; Simon Business School, University of Rochester, Rochester, New York 14627
abstract: This paper presents a scalable, nonparametric approach to estimating point-wise price elasticities designed for real-time pricing decisions. A key challenge in these settings is correcting for price endogeneity while remaining computationally efficient. We address this by leveraging nonparametric control functions to decompose the identification of causal elasticities into a sequence of scalable intermediate prediction tasks. We implement this framework with bootstrap averaged (bagged) nearest neighbors, which admits a closed-form representation that enables scalable, real-time implementation. We establish uniform consistency of our estimator and show in Monte Carlo simulations that it robustly recovers local elasticities across a diverse range of data-generating processes. We demonstrate the method’s practical usefulness by applying it to the New York City ride-sharing market, recovering substantial spatial-temporal heterogeneity in price elasticity and updating citywide elasticity estimates in less than one minute, which provide a “just-in-time” input for algorithmic pricing systems. This paper was accepted by Raphael Thomadsen, marketing. Funding: J. Wang acknowledges financial support from the Research Grants Council of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, China [Grant 14508924]. title: Breaking Gender Norms: A Dynamic Perspective on Entering Gender-Atypical Occupations
authors: Sophie Schellhammer; Florian Kunze
affiliations: University of Konstanz
abstract: Occupational gender segregation remains a defining feature of labor markets worldwide, and efforts to recruit individuals into gender-atypical occupations often fail because newcomers drop out shortly after entry. Understanding what drives this early attrition requires examining the day-to-day experiences of newcomers whose gender is underrepresented in their occupation, especially during the critical first weeks of organizational socialization. Integrating role congruity theory with a dynamic work-events perspective, we propose that gender-atypical newcomers experience an intensifying trajectory of perceived negative work events over time, and that this intensifying trajectory undermines their task mastery and heightens their turnover intention. Results from a longitudinal field study applying a repeated-measures design to 673 newcomers across 88 occupations over 12 weeks support these predictions. Newcomers working in gender-atypical occupations experienced a significant increase in negative work events over time, with this effect being significantly stronger for men in female-dominated occupations than for women in male-dominated occupations. Furthermore, steeper negative work event trajectories were associated with lower task mastery and higher turnover intentions. These findings advance dissimilarity research by uncovering the dynamic mechanism through which gender dissimilarity translates into adverse adjustment outcomes and contribute to the anchoring events literature by demonstrating the disproportionate and lasting influence of early negative experiences at the very outset of a professional career.

title: Juking the Stats: Policing, Misreporting, and Policy Evaluation
authors: Michael Gibilisco; Carlo M Horz
affiliations: California Insitute of Technology; Washington University in Saint Louis
abstract: Abstract We analyze a game-theoretic model of crime and crime reporting to study the quality of crime statistics. An offender potentially engages in illicit behavior; an enforcer chooses effort and how to report outcomes. Because of signaling concerns, the enforcer may misreport. We show that multiple equilibria can exist and characterize when crime is under- or overreported. Increasing the enforcer’s costs of data manipulation can backfire, increasing misreporting in crime statistics. When calculating treatment effects of parameter changes, the effect on reported statistics will not equal the effect on true statistics, and the true effect can be under- or overestimated.

title: ‘Every one should be marked as happy’. Challenging normalisation and expanding the sociozoological imagination in a Qualitative Behaviour Assessment of laboratory mouse welfare
authors: Maisie Tomlinson
affiliations: Department of Sociology, University of Manchester, UK
abstract: This paper explores Qualitative Behaviour Assessment’s (QBA) challenge to what Arluke and Sanders call the ‘sociozoologic scale’ of the hierarchical, moral categorisation of animals. QBA is a professional animal welfare methodology which invites assessors to interpret animals’ emotional expressions (e.g. ‘playful’ or ‘depressed’) through a subjectivist, interpretivist lens. Drawing on ethnographic research in a UK animal research facility, I explore the significance of QBA’s ‘Free Choice Profiling’ instruction to observe video footage of the same species across different environmental contexts before developing and using the tool. Its value is demonstrated through an instance where the instruction was poorly followed, leading to the problematic ‘normalisation’ of mouse behaviour. Drawing on C. Wright Mills’ ‘sociological imagination’, I argue that QBA’s directions invite an expanded ‘sociozoological imagination’, with relevance for a more reflexive, accountable and relational social science.

title: Reconfiguring Boundaries: Institutional Work and the Dynamic Construction of Hybridity in Local Government
authors: Lode De Waele; Kim Loyens; Caitlin McMullin
affiliations: Utrecht University School of Governance, Utrecht University , Bijlhouwerstraat 6, 3511 ZC Utrecht, the; University of Antwerp Politics & Public Governance Research Group, , Sint-Jacobstraat 2, 2000 Antwerp,; Roskilde University Department of Social Sciences and Business, , Universitetsvej 1, DK-4000 Roskilde,
abstract: Abstract This study examines how public managers shape intra-public hybridity when a reform requires two public organizations with different administrative traditions and professional orientations to integrate. We study the political and administrative integration of Flemish municipalities and Public Centres for Social Welfare (PCSWs), drawing on 35 interviews across 13 local government cases collected in 2018 and 2022. Using an institutional work perspective, we compare how actors used regulative, normative, and cultural-cognitive actions to integrate—or deliberately keep separate—structures, routines, and identities. The cases developed four hybrid forms: blended, segmented, segregated, and blocked. Blended cases were associated with institutionally broader combinations of work across organizational domains, whereas segmented and segregated cases showed more bounded efforts and blocked cases featured deliberate withholding of integrative work. These findings show that the same formal mandate can produce different organizational outcomes because local actors vary in the scope and combination of the work through which they enact it. The study advances a process-oriented account of intra-public hybridity and identifies deliberate withholding as a distinct mechanism of boundary maintenance.

title: Linking Women’s Equality With Government Integrity: Can Gender Budgeting Curb Corruption?
authors: Marjorie De la Cruz; Milena I. Neshkova; Yoon‐Jung Choi
affiliations: Department of Public Policy and Administration School of International and Public Affairs Florida International University Miami Florida USA
abstract: ABSTRACT Policies addressing gender inequality have increasingly been linked to more ethical governance, as women tend to be disproportionately burdened by corruption compared to men. One such policy is gender budgeting, an innovative approach to resource allocation that considers the impact of government spending on women and other underrepresented groups. Despite the growing popularity worldwide, we know little about its effectiveness in curbing corruption. This study evaluates the impact of gender budgeting on grand (political) and petty (bureaucratic) corruption using difference‐in‐differences estimations across a panel of 136 countries from 1980 to 2023. The results reveal a significant reduction in petty corruption, as gender budgeting improves the impartiality of public bureaucracies. Heterogeneity analyses also indicate a decrease in grand corruption, but only in countries with adequate levels of budget transparency, oversight, and public participation. The study highlights the far‐reaching consequences of gender reforms for the quality of governance.

title: Refine more, explore less? How buyer–supplier inventor ties shape innovation search outcomes
authors: Bowen Zheng; Baozhuang Niu
affiliations: School of Business Administration, South China University of Technology , ,
abstract: Purpose Innovation in supply chains depends on technical coordination between buyers and suppliers, yet close coordination may constrain a firm's ability to search beyond established supplier interfaces. This study examines how inventor ties shape buyers' exploitative and exploratory innovation as distinct outcomes of innovation search. Inventor ties refer to overlaps in inventor identities across buyer and supplier patent records. We further examine whether these relationships vary with technological distance and supplier concentration. Design/methodology/approach We use a panel of 1,872 buyer–supplier dyad-year observations from Chinese A-share listed firms over the period 2007–2024 and estimate firm fixed-effects models. The analysis examines the relationships between inventor ties and two innovation outcomes within firms. It also tests the moderating effects of technological distance and supplier concentration. Findings Inventor ties are positively associated with exploitative innovation but negatively associated with exploratory innovation. Technological distance weakens the positive relationship with exploitative innovation and weakens the negative relationship with exploratory innovation. Supplier concentration strengthens both relationships because a concentrated supply base reduces the buyer's flexibility to redirect innovation across alternative supplier interfaces. Originality/value The study shows that inventor ties can facilitate interface-based refinement while also reinforcing innovation lock-in. It advances operations and supply chain management research by explaining how technical actors embedded in buyer–supplier interfaces shape firms' innovation portfolios, thereby linking supply chain coordination mechanisms to the exploration-exploitation trade-off.

title: In from the cold: intermediary strategies for sourcing from a stigmatized supply network after a geopolitical shift
authors: Farmon Asadov; Quynh Do; Mark Stevenson
affiliations: Department of Management Science, Lancaster University Management School , ,
abstract: Purpose As geopolitical shifts reshape global sourcing, firms increasingly reconsider suppliers in regions previously excluded by sanctions, boycotts and other geopolitical instruments. Such exclusions often leave a lasting stigma, and suppliers in these regions struggle to establish legitimacy as buyers discount their signals. This research examines how supply chain intermediaries undertake legitimation work to overcome suppliers' legitimacy deficits that otherwise deter reintegration. Design/methodology/approach We conduct a longitudinal multiple-case study in the Uzbekistan cotton–textile industry (2019–2026), a revelatory instance of reintegration after the lifting of a global boycott. The three cases are buyer–supplier relationships in this setting, each brokered by the same three intermediaries. We draw abductively on 46 interviews with buyers, suppliers and intermediaries, over 80 h of observations, and 2,231 pages of archival documents. Findings Uzbek suppliers face three legitimacy deficits: cognitive illegibility, pragmatic incompatibility and moral fragility. In response, intermediaries employ three strategies: (1) cognitive bridging to render suppliers comprehensible; (2) network grafting to make exchange workable; and (3) norm cascading to embed global standards into supplier practices so that compliance becomes credible and durable. Together, these strategies move suppliers from exclusion to accepted sourcing relationships with global buyers. Originality/value We extend supply chain geopolitics research to reintegration, showing how a previously excluded region re-enters global sourcing following a geopolitical shift. We theorize intermediated legitimation as the mechanism enabling this, with legitimation work shifting to the intermediary. Contrary to the sequence assumed in prior literature, cognitive legitimacy emerges as the gateway to pragmatic and moral legitimacy.

title: Sorting inequality: The dynamics of occupational segregation and the Black–White earnings gap in Canada
authors: Antong Hou; Rupa Banerjee; Senanu Kwasi Kutor
affiliations: Faculty of Arts and Sciences, Harvard College, Cambridge, MA, USA; Ted Rogers School of Management, Toronto Metropolitan University, ON, Canada
abstract: Wage inequality between Black and White workers has remained persistent in recent decades across Western countries. This study examines how changes in occupational sorting and within-occupation wage disparities have contributed to the Black–White earnings gap over the past two decades in Canada. Using Social Dominance Theory as a framework, the analysis reveals that the wage gap linked to occupational sorting increased in the private sector for both Black men and women and increased in the public sector for Black men. The within-occupation wage gap also increased in the private sector for Black men. These findings suggest that efforts to reduce Black workers’ wage disparities have achieved only moderate success, primarily in narrowing within-occupation wage gaps, particularly for Black women in the public sector. The study highlights the limitations of current employment equity legislation in addressing structural and systemic inequalities, particularly those that sustain hierarchy-enhancing mechanisms such as differential occupational sorting.

title: The practical logic of professional aspiration among young Chinese actors
authors: Jinzhang Zhou
affiliations: Capital Normal University, Beijing, China
abstract: Amid China’s economic transformation and the expansion of digital platform capitalism, young actors increasingly navigate conditions of precarity. Existing research often focuses on structural issues like economic hardship or critiques of platform capital, overlooking how these practitioners form their identities and find meaning. Drawing on theories of precarity and aspiration, this article uses qualitative data to reveal a practical logic of professional aspiration articulated through three concepts: ‘ zhi ’ (oriented persistence), ‘ shi ’ (situational momentum) and ‘ bian ’ (co-creative transformation). This framework allows actors to navigate highly unstable labour markets and construct meaningful work–life structures. The study contributes both empirically and theoretically: first, it offers an analytical perspective rooted in Chinese practical wisdom for understanding the subjectivity and agency of workers in precarious employment; second, it enriches precarity studies by demonstrating how the structural conditions of work can be reconciled with the complexity and diversity of lived experience.

title: Desired and undesired identities: A study of Irish peacekeepers
authors: Angela McGinn; Andrew D. Brown
affiliations: Department of Adult and Community Education, Maynooth University, Ireland; School of Management, University of Bath, UK
abstract: Based on an interview study of 48 Irish Defence Forces officers, this article analyses how peacekeepers constructed both positively valenced desired and negatively valenced undesired occupational identities. It demonstrates how interviewees drew on their ‘Irishness’ – their shared understandings of their history, pragmatism and character – as orienting cues to construct desired identities as neutral, flexible and empathetic, and undesired identities as lacking confidence, rule-bending and needing to be liked. This study makes two principal sets of contributions. First, it argues that desired and undesired identities are constructed in relation to each other and are mutually constitutive. Second, it theorises officers’ work on desired identities as a project of moralisation that was challenged by their construction of undesired identities.

title: Agency, care and constraint: Maternal self-employment and the reframing of the adaptive woman
authors: Lauren Bari; Siva Shaangari Seathu Raman
affiliations: Department of Work and Employment Studies, University of Limerick, Ireland; School of Healthcare Management, Royal College of Surgeons, Dublin, Ireland
abstract: Recent years have seen growth in freelance and solo self-employment among women, particularly those with children, reflecting changing labour market conditions and the persistent demands of care. Drawing on interviews with self-employed mothers, this paper examines solo self-employment as a distinctive site of gendered adaptation and revisits Hakim’s concept of the adaptive woman in contemporary labour markets. Across social positions, participants described similar experiences of the mental load, gendered expectations and continual negotiation of work around caregiving. Yet rather than renouncing ambition, participants described continually seeking ways to integrate meaningful work with maternal care. The paper therefore extends Hakim’s concept by reframing adaptation not as a stable preference defined by compromise but as an enduring social process through which women organise productive work around care.

title: Moral Licensing Revisited: CSR and Cybersecurity‐related Disclosure After COP21
authors: Vu Quang Trinh; Teng Li; Marwa Elnahass; Ngan Duong Cao
affiliations: Newcastle University Business School, Newcastle University Newcastle upon Tyne NE1 7RU UK; Essex Business School University of Essex Colchester CO4 3SQ UK; Department of Accounting and Finance King Fahd University of Petroleum & Minerals Dhahran Saudi Arabia; Interdisciplinary Research Center for Hydrogen Technologies and Carbon Management King Fahd University of Petroleum & Minerals Dhahran Saudi Arabia; University of Bath School of Management Bath BA2 7AY UK
abstract: Abstract Using a sample of U.S. S&P 100 firms, we examine the relationship between firms’ CSR and cybersecurity‐related disclosure, exploiting the 2015 Paris Climate Conference (COP21) as an institutional shock in a difference‐in‐differences design. We find that, prior to COP21, firms’ aggregated environmental and social (E&S) profiles, and environmental (E) profiles are negatively but not significantly associated with cybersecurity‐related disclosure, whereas social (S) profiles exhibit a significantly negative association. Drawing on moral licensing theory, we argue that firm leaders who perceive their firms as having accumulated sufficient moral capital through CSR engagement may feel less compelled to respond proactively to emerging stakeholder expectations in non‐traditional responsibility domains such as cybersecurity. Following COP21, however, firms with stronger aggregated E&S, E, and S profiles increase their cybersecurity‐related disclosure. We interpret COP21 as an institutional inflection point that intensified scrutiny and strengthened evaluative standards surrounding corporate sustainability, thereby diminishing the protective value of previously accrued moral credentials. Under heightened accountability, firm leaders appear more inclined to reaffirm a responsible organizational identity through greater transparency and responsiveness to stakeholder information demands. Overall, our evidence suggests that greater cybersecurity‐related disclosure may help firms signal their commitment to cybersecurity and reinforce their socially legitimate identity.

title: Parsimonious theorizing
authors: Diego Jannace; Saeid Kazemi; Arnaldo Camuffo
affiliations: Entrepreneurship and Family Enterprise INSEAD Singapore Singapore; ION Management Science Lab‐SDA Bocconi Bocconi University Milan Italy; Department of Economics and Decision Sciences HEC Paris Paris France; Department of Management and Technology Bocconi University Milan Italy
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Entrepreneurs act on theories of value, and the theory‐based view favors simplicity. Yet a theory can be too thin to guide action or too heavy to carry, and simplicity cannot tell which. We model a theory as bundles linking attempted actions, uncertain implementation states, and external conditions to a focal outcome, and make its structure a choice variable. Parsimony then calls for optimal rather than minimal complexity: structure whose contribution to the value of acting justifies its carrying cost. Under the model's assumptions, optimal complexity rises with value at stake, representational capacity, and domain knowledge, and falls with bundle overlap. Theories also change. The entrepreneur's theory shapes her awareness, so some bundles are worth carrying for what they open, while commitments make revision path dependent. Managerial Summary Entrepreneurs often need to explain a future that does not yet exist: what they will try, what must work, and why customers, partners, or investors should care. We show how to weigh the value of linked actions, their possible results, and outside conditions against the effort of understanding, communicating, and testing them. More detail is worthwhile when the potential payoff is greater, the entrepreneur knows the business better, or the team can handle complexity; overlapping ideas add less. As evidence accumulates, the theory may need to expand, shrink, or be rebuilt. Some ideas are worth keeping because they reveal new possibilities. Earlier investments can make changes costly, so a failed test may call for reshaping the idea rather than abandoning it.

title: XBRL adoption and SEC monitoring
authors: Minjae Koo; Yinqi Zhang; Meiling Zhao; Yuping Zhao
abstract: Abstract We examine how disclosure processing costs influence SEC monitoring of firm disclosures by leveraging the mandatory adoption of XBRL—a digital reporting language designed to reduce these costs. Post adoption, both the frequency and quality of SEC comment letters for 10-K filings increase. Additional tests suggest that XBRL enhances SEC monitoring through three channels. First, automated data extraction improves review efficiency, as reflected in more timely comment letters and greater XBRL benefits when the SEC faces tighter resource constraints or uses XBRL analytical tools. Second, standardized reporting strengthens the SEC’s benchmarking ability: firms using more standardized tags and tags more comparable to those of industry peers benefit more. Third, XBRL facilitates SEC scrutiny of complex reporting issues, yielding more frequent and higher-quality comments on noncore earnings accounts and for firms with more footnote tags or complex filings. Overall, our evidence suggests that reduced disclosure processing costs enhance the SEC’s regulatory monitoring.

title: Merit or Whiteness? Tracing Racial Bias in the Selection of Individual UN Human Rights Experts
authors: Andrea Liese; Andreas Johannes Ullmann
affiliations: Universität Potsdam
abstract: Abstract Do race or merit make an international expert? While existing research has uncovered epistemic biases related to gender and professions, racial bias in international organisations’ expert selection has not been captured. We argue that signalling whiteness is central to the certification of expertise because expert status is built on racialised structures of epistemic power. Examining individual-level data from 2,053 applications and selection outcomes across several stages in 124 decision rounds between 2011 and 2024 for the United Nations’ Special Procedures, we show that expert selection is subject to racial bias when candidates are chosen for in-person interviews and how markers of whiteness and merit overlap. We also find that non-white experts can increase their chances of being selected when they possess higher merit-related credentials than their white counterparts. Our research informs scholarship on racism in international relations, the production of expertise in international organisations, and human rights politics.

title: Regional Deprivation, Individual Prospects, and Political Resentment
authors: Giovanni Facchini; Anja Neundorf; Sergi Pardos-Prado; Cecilia Testa
affiliations: University of Nottingham and Centre for Economic Policy Research; University of Glasgow
abstract: Abstract Regional economic conditions are well-established determinants of the geography of political resentment. However, regions are not homogeneous, and the mechanisms through which local economies affect individual political attitudes are unclear. We argue that feelings of relative deprivation are shaped by how personal prospects are tied to regional conditions, and that the interaction between subjective individual and regional deprivation affects perceptions of shared struggle and systemic unfairness. Through a large-scale survey experiment in Britain addressing geographical self-selection, we provide causal evidence that poor individuals in poor regions express political resentment, whereas in affluent regions the political attitudes of poor and wealthy individuals are indistinguishable. Our findings stress (1) the importance of egocentric mechanisms whereby local economies shape individual prospects; (2) the significance of subjective beliefs over objective information on deprivation; (3) the mobilization potential of highlighting regional deprivation by political entrepreneurs; and (4) the relevance of place-based policies to mitigate political discontent.

title: Breaking into the Public Sphere: How Protest Tactics Shape Media Visibility
authors: Michael Jacobs
affiliations: ETH Zurich: Eidgenossische Technische Hochschule Zurich
abstract: Abstract Getting heard is a crucial first step for protesters to influence policy and public opinion. How can protest organisers boost their coverage in the media? This study provides new evidence on this question, based on a decade of UK environmental and economic protests from 2010 to 2020 ( N = 1,708). Relying on protest groups’ social media streams as trace data, I introduce a computer-assisted method for constructing a media-independent protest event dataset. Using a ‘within-group’ design, I provide a sharper test of the causal effects of tactical choices compared to previous studies. I find that confrontational elements, such as disruption and arrests, are the strongest predictors, more than doubling the expected magnitude of coverage. I also find that right-leaning (ideologically unsympathetic) outlets are more responsive to confrontational elements than left-leaning (ideologically sympathetic) outlets, which suggests that disruptive tactics affect the composition as well as the size of a protest’s audience.

INO volume 80 issue 4 Cover and Back matter
The Dependence Dilemma: Engagement, Vulnerability, and the Politics of Derisking
authors: Brett V. Benson; Haonan Dong; Bradley C. Smith
affiliations: Vanderbilt University; Princeton University
abstract: Abstract What makes economic interdependence a force for peace rather than a source of strategic vulnerability? We argue that interdependence generates both pacifying opportunity costs and dangerous dependence, and the tension between these two forces is the key to understanding when economic engagement promotes peace and when it provokes war. We develop a dynamic model of economic dependence and conflict that generates both the pacifying and conflict-inducing effects of interdependence within a single unified framework. We show that states use “derisking” as a strategic middle path, selectively restricting economic engagement to reset future leverage without destroying the gains from exchange that make peace valuable. The theory explains why dependence-driven wars are rare yet possible. Forward-looking leaders prefer incurring the costs of economic restraint to the catastrophic risks of conflict. When derisking is structurally foreclosed or restrictions destroy too much economic value, the commitment problem cannot be managed through policy and preventive war may occur.

title: Territory Without Centralization: Conflicting Spatial Ideologies of the Shogunate, Domains, and Villages in Early Modern Japan
authors: Naosuke Mukoyama
affiliations: University of Tokyo
abstract: Abstract This article reconceptualizes the formation of territory by examining early modern Japan, showing that territory can emerge through bottom-up processes without centralization. Contrary to dominant narratives based on European history that portray territory as a product of top-down projects, the Japanese case reveals that multiple levels of political actors—the Tokugawa shogunate, individual domains, and village communities—held competing spatial ideologies and engaged in struggles over how space should be organized and governed, and as a result, territory emerged without centralization. The shogunate sought to impose a vision of a unified territory through land surveys and repeated production of provincial maps. However, because it lacked the capacity to carry out these projects directly, implementation depended on domains, inadvertently strengthening their territorial demarcation and autonomy. Yet domains themselves could not fully impose their spatial conceptions onto the population. Because land surveys focused only on cultivated fields, the delineation of boundaries in uncultivated areas was driven by peasants whose need for access to common resources such as grasslands and timber motivated numerous inter-village disputes. Through boundary disputes, villages played a central role in defining the borders that ultimately structured domanial territories. This article contributes to international relations scholarship by revising the dominant state-centric view of territory and state formation, casting doubt on the effectiveness of war making and map making in the process of state formation, demonstrating that territorial formation need not coincide with sovereignty, and advancing our understanding of non-European historical international order.
